paras: The threatened lynching of Gent Jenkins was a proposed mob action in Muskogee, Oklahoma, in August 1915 against a Black man arrested after the hatchet murder of white grocer Wm. B. Province. According to the Muskogee Cimeter, a Black weekly, the forming mob dissolved after police and the sheriff warned it would meet deadly force, and Jenkins was discharged. Weeks later the victim's widow was charged with the murder.

Province was attacked with a hatchet in his store on the outskirts of Muskogee shortly after noon on Wednesday, August 11, 1915, and died about three hours later. A dispatch printed in the Daily Ardmoreite said he murmured with his last breath that a white man had struck the blow, and called it the third hatchet murder in the city in little more than a year.

Police arrested a Black man who gave the name J. Jenkins only minutes after the crime was discovered, and a neighbor said she had seen a Black man enter the store at noon. The Cimeter, which named him Gent Jenkins and also spelled it "Jinkins," reported that soon after the arrest a rumor spread that a lynching be proposed. In its account, Chief of Police Depew and his force and Sheriff Barger and his deputies, backed by "the best class of white and colored citizens," let it be known that a mob would furnish "lots of material for the undertaker," and "the embryo mob dissolved." Jenkins was then released, the officers having concluded from the dying man's statement that he was not the killer.

The investigation moved elsewhere: County Attorney Fred P. Branson questioned about forty witnesses in a secret inquisition, and Tulsa police held a Black couple, Harry and Emma Brown, as possible suspects. On September 2 Province's widow was arrested and charged with first-degree murder after a boy identified the hatchet as one kept at the store, contradicting her testimony at the coroner's inquest. She pleaded not guilty, and no report of a trial was found in the coverage.

The lynching talk appears only in the Muskogee Cimeter of August 14, under the headline "Murder Most Foul." The paper insisted that whoever the killer was, "be he white black or red," should be punished "as the law directs," and said it was proud of a city that had always stood against mob violence. White Oklahoma papers followed the murder as the work of a "hatchet fiend" and later as a case against the widow, mentioning Jenkins only once, as a suspect released, and never mentioning a mob.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Gent Jenkins
bases: The only account of mob action (A2) describes a proposed lynching of an arrested Black suspect that dissolved after officers threatened force; no one was harmed.

No one was killed: according to A2 the 'embryo mob' dissolved after officers warned it off, so this is at most a threatened lynching; the proposed action was extralegal punishment of a murder suspect (A2).
Only the Muskogee Cimeter (A2) reports the lynching talk; the white wire report (A1) confirms the arrest and release of a Black man named Jenkins but says nothing of a mob.

accounts.label: Black local weekly
accounts.gist: After Jenkins's arrest a lynching was proposed, but police and sheriff, backed by white and colored citizens, threatened that a mob would supply the undertaker, and the 'embryo mob dissolved'; Jenkins was discharged.

accounts.label: Wire report from Muskogee
accounts.gist: Police arrested a negro giving the name J. Jenkins minutes after the murder was discovered but released him, since the dying grocer said a white man struck the blow; nothing about a mob.

framing.detail: Under 'MURDER MOST FOUL' the Cimeter demanded the killer, 'be he white black or red', be punished 'as the law directs' and praised Muskogee for standing against mob violence.
The Ardmoreite's 'HATCHET FIEND IS AGAIN BUSY IN MUSKOGEE' treated the arrest of the 'negro' Jenkins as a passing detail and reported no lynching talk.

conflicts.note: The Ardmoreite says the man 'gave the name of J. Jenkins'; the local Cimeter, which spells it both ways in one article, gives a first name.

versions.value: Twenty-sixth and Okmulgee streets (the Province home)

conflicts.note: Minor; A6 refers to the home, which may differ from the store.

info: The murder of W. B. Province was on Wednesday, Aug. 11, 1915; the arrest of Jenkins came minutes after the crime was discovered and the lynching talk 'soon after' the arrest.
Muskogee; Province's grocery at 22nd and Okmulgee (Cimeter), on the outskirts of the city (Ardmoreite); a later report puts the Province home at Twenty-sixth and Okmulgee streets.
Gent Jenkins (also 'Jinkins'), described as a negro; the Ardmoreite gives 'J. Jenkins'.
Arrested as a suspect in the hatchet murder of white grocer Wm. B. Province; released/discharged.
An unnamed 'embryo mob'; its makeup and size are not given.
Jenkins was discharged; police doubted he was the killer because Province said with his last breath that a white man struck him.
